title: Emergency/Standby Power Systems Fundamentals
summary: Understand the standby power systems that carry a facility through a utility outage.
description: Standby power systems — generators, transfer switches, and the sequencing logic between them — are what actually carries a facility through a utility outage. This course covers standby power system fundamentals: automatic transfer switches, sequencing, and the maintenance that keeps them ready. You'll leave able to explain the failure points most likely to prevent a successful transfer, before they're tested by a real outage.
why_it_matters: When utility power fails, the UPS carries the load for minutes. Standby generators and automatic transfer switches (ATSs) keep the facility running beyond that. If a generator fails to start, a transfer switch sticks or the sequencing logic is wrong, the UPS batteries run down and the site goes dark. Standby power systems are covered by several standards. The National Electrical Code separates emergency systems (Article 700), legally required standby (Article 701) and optional standby (Article 702), and NFPA 110 covers the performance, testing and maintenance of emergency and standby power systems. This course covers how standby systems are laid out, how ATSs work, how sequencing and load coordination are set up, and the maintenance that keeps the system ready.
audience: Facilities technicians responsible for standby and emergency power systems.
prerequisites: No prior certification required. Relevant equipment exposure is helpful.
learning_outcomes: Understand how standby power systems sequence during a utility outage
Explain automatic transfer switch operation and testing
Apply maintenance practices that keep standby systems ready
Recognize the failure points most likely to prevent a successful transfer

faqs.question: What does an automatic transfer switch do?
faqs.answer: An ATS monitors the normal power source. When it fails, the ATS signals the generator to start and transfers the load once generator voltage and frequency are stable. When utility power returns, it transfers the load back and lets the generator cool down.

faqs.question: What is the difference between open and closed transition transfer?
faqs.answer: Open transition briefly disconnects the load before connecting it to the other source (break-before-make). Closed transition briefly parallels the two sources so the load is not interrupted (make-before-break), which requires additional controls and utility approval in many cases.

faqs.question: How often should standby generators be tested?
faqs.answer: NFPA 110 requires regular exercising and inspection, commonly monthly under load for Level 1 systems, plus periodic longer tests. The exact requirements depend on the system's classification and local rules, which the Maintenance for Readiness module explains.
